doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Repertoire and the college's indifference to jazz
summary: Tunes the band played, the college's bemused attitude, and learning harmony in Berrian Shute's music appreciation course.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Give me two or three songs that would have been on your playlist.

Well we played all those standard things, “Muskrat Ramble” and “The Saints Go Marching In,” and “Black and Blue” and oh the blues of course and probably “Memphis Blues,” I can’t remember exactly. There was one we used to do all the time called “She Looks Like Helen Brown.” I’ve never heard of it since. I could probably still play it if I had to.
Did the college have any input, any opinion, any other thing to do with what you were doing?
No the college was bemused. The college thought jazz, well that’s a rather funny sort of thing and we don’t know anything about it and they had no interest in it really at all.

Well I took the music appreciation course. There was a guy called Berrian Shute, and he was very good. It was a very good course and I learned chord changes, I learned harmony, I learned basic Western harmony from this course. And that was how I began to get my changes together and I realized hey, there’s a whole scheme here that you could know. And so I — but they had no interest in jazz whatever. None. This was an odd little hobby like who knows what, collecting pottery or something or other that some of the students had. That was alright but nobody was going to encourage it.
